pairs.rationale: The Judean teachers make Mosaic circumcision necessary for salvation. Galatians states whole-law obligation for one receiving circumcision and warns those seeking justification by law of separation from Christ. Its distinct clauses and conditions remain a separate argument rather than a verbatim report of these teachers or a blanket claim about every circumstance of circumcision.

Both passages describe Paul going to Jerusalem with Barnabas and presenting concerns about the Gentile gospel to leadership. Galatians adds Titus, a revelation and a private presentation; Acts describes an appointed delegation after public dispute. Their visits and chronology are not forcibly identified.

Paul and Barnabas earlier report to the Antioch Church that God opened a door of faith to the Gentiles; here their account of Gentile conversion brings joy in Phoenicia and Samaria. These are different report settings, not one gathering or a second account of every conversion.

Both Jerusalem arrivals involve welcome and an account of what God did through the mission. Acts15 names Paul and Barnabas reporting to the Church, apostles and elders; Acts21 describes a later arrival and Paul reporting to James with the elders. The visits and participants remain distinct.

The Pharisaic believers demand circumcision and keeping the law of Moses. The later Jerusalem statement recalls the decision sent to believing Gentiles as four abstentions, without making this proposed circumcision requirement part of its list. The proposal and the reported decision are distinguished.

Apostles and elders gather over the Gentile-law question here. At the later Jerusalem visit James and the elders hear Paul, discuss concerns about Moses and Jewish practice, and recall the Gentile decision. This is a later meeting referring to the earlier decision, not the same session.

Peter recalls his earlier role in Gentiles hearing the gospel and believing. In the Cornelius scene Peter speaks about the appointed judge and forgiveness for believers, and the Spirit falls on those hearing him. That narrative supplies the earlier preaching setting without repeating every word of this recollection.

Peter interprets the Spirit gift to the Gentiles as God bearing witness to them, with his stated comparison just as to us. Acts10 narrates the Spirit falling on the hearers and Peter explicitly saying they received the Spirit just as his group did. The heart-knowing description belongs to this council speech.

Here Peter speaks of no distinction and hearts cleansed by faith. His earlier defense speaks of God giving the same gift as to those believing in Jesus, followed by the hearers recognizing Gentile repentance leading to life. The heart-cleansing formulation is not quoted from that earlier account.

Peter objects to placing an unbearable yoke upon the disciples in this circumcision dispute. Galatians warns against a yoke of slavery and connects receiving circumcision with obligation to the whole law. The speakers and arguments differ; the shared yoke image does not erase those distinctions.

Peter states that his group and the Gentiles are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus in the same way. Ephesians describes salvation by grace through faith as God’s gift rather than from works. The letter does not repeat the council speech or its comparison of the two groups.

Barnabas and Paul report signs and wonders God did among Gentiles through them. The Iconium narrative describes both Jews and Greeks believing and the Lord granting signs and wonders through the missionaries’ hands. This is a concrete earlier example, not an exhaustive identification of all the reported signs.

James speaks after the mission report at this Jerusalem gathering. In the later Jerusalem visit Paul goes to James with all the elders and reports God’s work among the Gentiles. The shared setting and role provide a leadership connection without identifying the two meetings or supplying James’s family relationship.

James summarizes the Gentile visitation just related by Simeon. Acts10 narrates Gentiles receiving the Spirit during Peter’s preaching and being ordered baptized in Jesus Christ’s name. The narrative is the earlier reception setting, not a verbatim statement that God took a people for His name.

James introduces agreement with the prophets, then cites the rebuilding of David’s tent and the nations seeking. Those linked images occur in the saved Greek-based Amos text. The introduction itself is James’s framing, and the source’s following wording is not made identical to Amos in every clause.

Both passages speak of raising or rebuilding David’s fallen tent and its damaged parts. Acts begins with a return after these things, whereas Amos begins on that day and speaks of rebuilding as in days of old. The quotation’s altered introduction and formulations remain visible.

The saved Amos text has remaining human beings and nations over whom God’s name is called seeking; Acts has the rest of humanity seeking the Lord and nations upon whom His name is called. Both end with the Lord’s doing, with their different explicit objects and wording retained.

The council quotation concludes with things known from long ago. Peter’s earlier speech describes the restoration of things God spoke through His holy prophets from long ago. This connects their long-ago prophetic framing, without claiming Acts3 is the quoted Amos line or that every restoration detail is restated here.

James judges that Gentiles turning to God should not be troubled. The later Jerusalem statement recalls the limited abstentions sent to believing Gentiles. The target records the decision’s requirements, rather than repeating James’s judgment word for word or eliminating its specific obligations.

Both lists address Gentile believers and name idol-related pollution or sacrifices, sexual immorality, strangled things and blood. The target recalls the sent decision with a different order and the more specific sacrificed-to-idols formulation; the lists are not silently rewritten to match.

James refers to Moses being read in synagogues every Sabbath. The Pisidian Antioch visit specifically narrates a Sabbath synagogue gathering followed by reading the law and prophets. That scene illustrates the reading practice without independently proving its antiquity or occurrence in every city.

The narrative names Judas called Barsabbas and Silas as the chosen envoys to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. The letter subsequently names Judas and Silas as sent to give the same message orally. These are the narrative selection and its written announcement, not independent attestations.

The Jerusalem writers address Gentile brothers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. The next journey reports handing on the Jerusalem apostles’ and elders’ decisions for observance in the cities. The target describes wider delivery rather than repeating this greeting or naming exactly the same recipients.

The letter says some from their company unsettled the recipients without instruction. The opening narrative records men coming from Judea with the circumcision-for-salvation teaching and the resulting dispute. The letter supplies the lack-of-authorization claim; the opening narrative does not independently state it.

The letter announces the united decision to choose men to accompany Barnabas and Paul. The narrative describes apostles, elders and the whole Church making that choice and names Judas and Silas. The written announcement and narrated selection belong to the same decision.

The letter commends Barnabas and Paul as men who gave over their lives for Jesus Christ’s name. Acts14 supplies a concrete danger to Paul, stoned and left for dead before he later departs with Barnabas. It does not say Barnabas was also stoned or exhaust all dangers covered by the commendation.

The letter promises Judas and Silas will report the message by word of mouth. The narrative later describes those same named prophets encouraging and strengthening the brothers with many words. It does not quote their whole oral report or equate every encouraging word with the letter text.

The letter attributes its limited burden to the Holy Spirit and the writers’ judgment. Acts16 reports handing on decisions made by the Jerusalem apostles and elders for observance. The later summary identifies the decision’s human leadership without repeating the letter’s Spirit attribution or its exact list.

Both accounts list idol sacrifices, blood, strangled things and sexual immorality as the Gentile requirements. The letter also includes the doing-well assurance and farewell, which the later recollection does not repeat. The shared list is a later internal recall, not an independent source for the original letter.

The chosen party reaches Antioch, gathers the multitude and delivers the letter. The earlier decision sends the named men to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas and gives the letter’s greeting. The arrival performs that particular commission; it does not reproduce all their travel details.

The Antioch hearers rejoice at the letter’s encouragement. Earlier along this same council journey the Gentile-conversion report brings joy to brothers in Phoenicia and Samaria. The occasions and audiences differ, but both positive responses concern reception of the Gentile mission.

Judas and Silas act as prophets strengthening the brothers at Antioch. The earlier narrative brings prophets from Jerusalem to Antioch and names Agabus’s famine prediction. These are different prophets and messages; the comparison does not make Judas or Silas the famine predictor.

The envoys are sent away to those who commissioned them, while the later departure notice has Paul choose Silas. The passages mark separate stages in Silas’s narrative; they do not explain an intervening return or authorize inserting the absent15:34 notice that he remained.

Paul and Barnabas remain at Antioch teaching and proclaiming with others. Earlier Barnabas brings Saul to Antioch and the two spend a year gathering with the Church and teaching. The earlier year is not imposed on this later stay, and the two visits are not merged.

Paul proposes revisiting the brothers where he and Barnabas preached. The earlier journey names their return through Lystra, Iconium and Antioch to strengthen disciples and appoint elders. That supplies the prior mission and follow-up setting, not a statement that the later proposed journey was already completed.

Barnabas wishes to take John called Mark. Acts12 had already named John called Mark accompanying Barnabas and Saul after their service. The repeated full designation and companions establish the narrative connection without identifying him as an unnamed Gospel author.

Paul’s objection recalls the man’s withdrawal in Pamphylia. The earlier travel narrative explicitly has John leave Paul’s company at Perga in Pamphylia and return to Jerusalem. It records the departure but does not supply his motive or decide the later dispute between Paul and Barnabas.

Barnabas now sails to Cyprus with Mark after separating from Paul. The earlier Cyprus mission has Barnabas and Saul sent out together and John as their assistant. The destination and companion connections are precise, while the journeys and the later sharp disagreement remain distinct.

Paul leaves with Silas entrusted by the brothers to the Lord’s grace. The earlier mission’s return to Antioch recalls where its workers had been entrusted to God’s grace. The formula connects successive missions without assigning the earlier party’s completed work to Silas.

Paul travels through Syria and Cilicia strengthening the Churches. Those two regions occur alongside Antioch in the letter’s named Gentile recipients. The shared regional setting links the follow-up journey and decision, without claiming this verse alone documents delivery to every recipient.

Acts introduces Timothy as the son of a believing Jewish woman and Greek father. The letter to Timothy recalls sincere faith in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice and in Timothy. It supplies maternal family names and faith, but does not repeat the father’s ethnicity or all details of this meeting.

Local brothers in Lystra and Iconium speak well of Timothy. Paul’s letter later commends Timothy’s sincere care and proven service with him for the gospel. These are different witnesses and occasions, not the same recommendation or proof of each local brother’s testimony.

Paul circumcises Timothy because of the local Jews who knew his father was Greek. In Galatians, Greek Titus is not compelled to be circumcised amid a dispute about freedom and false brothers. The men and circumstances differ; the explicit local motive is not replaced with an invented universal policy or a harmonizing chronology.

The travelers hand on the decisions of the Jerusalem apostles and elders for observance. The letter gives that decision’s limited necessary abstentions and its Spirit-and-writers attribution. This is transmission of the earlier decision, not a second independently produced list.

Both narrative summaries describe the Church or Churches being strengthened or built up and increasing. Acts16 specifies strength in faith and daily numerical growth; Acts9 locates peace, fear of the Lord and Spirit encouragement in Judea, Galilee and Samaria. Those locations and narrative features are not copied into this later summary.

The Holy Spirit prevents speaking in Asia, then the Spirit of Jesus does not permit entry into Bithynia. These are successive restrictions within one journey, with different regions and the actual Spirit designations preserved rather than normalized.

The Bithynia attempt is not permitted by the Spirit of Jesus; the preceding notice says the Holy Spirit had prevented speech in Asia. The related journey restrictions have different objects and regions, and neither verse supplies an unreported motive for them.

Acts brings Paul’s party through Mysia to Troas before the Macedonian vision. Paul’s letter describes another Troas-to-Macedonia movement, with an opened gospel door and concern over missing Titus. The shared route is compared without making the vision and Titus concern one departure or the same occasion.

Paul’s night vision here shows a Macedonian man asking help. The later Corinth vision has the Lord encourage Paul to speak without fear and promises His presence. The vision scenes differ in speaker and purpose; the Macedonian man is not identified as the Lord or an angel.

After Paul’s vision the narrating group concludes God called them to evangelize Macedonia. In the earlier mission the Holy Spirit directly names Barnabas and Saul for the work and they are sent out. An inference from a vision is not rewritten as the same quoted command or the same missionary party.

This itinerary sails from Troas by Samothrace to Neapolis before reaching Philippi. The later itinerary sails from Philippi to Troas in five days. The endpoints connect the journeys, while direction, intermediate places and timing remain distinct and no unreported route is supplied.

The travelers arrive at Philippi, described here as a Macedonian district city and colony. Paul and Timothy’s letter addresses the saints in Philippi with overseers and deacons. The city links narrative mission and letter audience; the greeting does not repeat the colony status or this stay’s duration.

At Philippi the group goes by the river where they think there is a place of prayer and addresses gathered women on the Sabbath. At Thessalonica Paul reasons in the synagogue for three Sabbaths. The different venues and audiences are retained, without inferring that Philippi had no synagogue or a particular population requirement.

The Lord opens Lydia’s heart to attend to Paul’s words; Jesus opens the disciples’ mind to understand the Scriptures in Luke. The shared divine opening concerns different recipients, objects and settings, and does not make Lydia one of those disciples or supply an unreported conversion mechanism.

Lydia and her household are baptized and she presses the missionaries to stay at her house. Later the jailer receives a household salvation promise, his household hears the word, his people are baptized and he hosts a meal. The situations and sequences differ, and neither household’s ages are supplied.

The divining slave girl earns much for her masters. The Ephesus disturbance later features craftsmen whose prosperity depends on Artemis shrines and who fear loss from Paul’s message. The commercial settings are connected without equating divination with the narrated manufacture of shrines or treating the craftsmen’s divine claims as the narrator’s endorsement.

The girl with the divining spirit calls the missionaries servants of God Most High who proclaim salvation. In Mark the man with an unclean spirit identifies Jesus as God’s Holy One before Jesus rebukes the spirit. The speakers, titles and recipients differ; neither comparison endorses divination as an authorized gospel ministry.

Paul commands the spirit to leave in Jesus Christ’s name and it leaves that hour. The seventy-two report to Jesus that demons submit in His name. Their general report and this individual narrated exorcism share the named authority, without making them one event or assigning the girl an unstated diagnosis.

The owners seize Paul and Silas when their hope of profit disappears. Demetrius later gathers the craftsmen and explicitly connects prosperity and the danger to their trade with opposition to Paul. Different cities, trades and reactions remain distinct; the passage does not add a motive beyond the stated profit concerns.

The Philippian accusers portray the missionaries as Jews disrupting the city. The Thessalonian accusers portray Paul’s party as upsetting the world and acting against Caesar by naming Jesus another king. These are different accusations before local authorities, not narrator endorsements or an ethnic judgment.

The owners claim Roman identity and forbidden customs; the later accusation claims the missionaries act against Caesar and speak of another king, Jesus. The civic appeals differ, and neither speech is converted into an independently verified statement of Roman law.

The magistrates order Paul and Silas beaten with rods. Paul’s letter recalls three occasions when he was beaten with rods. The narrative supplies a concrete example of that category of suffering, while the letter neither names Philippi here nor identifies the other two occasions.

Acts describes many blows and imprisonment at Philippi. The letter recalls having suffered and been shamefully treated in Philippi before speaking the gospel to the Thessalonians amid struggle. The recollection matches the location and suffering without restating the jailer’s orders or every prison detail.

Paul and Silas are placed in the inner prison with feet in stocks. Peter’s earlier imprisonment has him sleeping between soldiers, bound with two chains and watched at the door. Both describe strong custody before extraordinary openings, but the restraints and prisoners are different.

Paul and Silas themselves pray and sing hymns while prisoners listen. During Peter’s confinement the Church makes earnest prayer to God for him. The prayer participants and location differ, and Peter’s account does not independently supply the singing or midnight timing.

The earthquake opens all doors and loosens everyone’s bonds. Peter’s chains fall and an iron gate opens during an angel-led departure. The mechanisms and scope differ: Acts16 does not narrate everyone escaping, while Peter actually follows the angel out.

The Philippian jailer supposes escape and prepares to kill himself; after Peter’s real escape Herod examines the guards and orders their execution. The feared and actual outcomes are distinct, and the comparison does not infer a universal penalty or that this jailer received such an order.

Paul prevents the jailer’s self-harm by announcing that all are still present. Herod instead has Peter’s guards led away for execution after Peter cannot be found. This contrasts the narrated treatment and outcome of keepers; it does not claim that the Philippian jailer was legally condemned or that Peter remained in custody.

The trembling jailer falls before Paul and Silas. Cornelius falls at Peter’s feet and bows, and Peter raises him while affirming that he too is human. The bodily response is comparable, but Acts16 does not expressly call the jailer’s action worship or repeat Peter’s words.

The jailer asks what he must do to be saved; the Pentecost hearers ask Peter and the apostles what they should do and receive a repentance-and-baptism answer. The questions arise in different situations, and the different stated answers are retained rather than replaced with one quotation.

Paul and Silas direct the jailer to believe in the Lord Jesus and speak of salvation for him and his household. John links belief in God’s Son with life and salvation rather than perishing or judgment. John does not repeat the household promise or establish that one person’s belief substitutes for every other household member’s response.

The missionaries speak the Lord’s word to the jailer and everyone in his house. Cornelius says the gathered group is before God to hear what the Lord commanded Peter, who then begins speaking. The households and speeches differ; no ages or identical membership of the audiences are assumed.

The jailer tends the missionaries’ wounds and he and all his people are baptized that night. Earlier Lydia attends to Paul and she and her household are baptized. These are two different Philippian households; only the jailer scene contains wound washing and night timing, and neither gives the household members’ ages.

After the baptism the jailer brings the missionaries into his house, serves food and rejoices with his household. Lydia earlier urges the missionaries to stay in her home after her household’s baptism. The hospitality corresponds, while the meal, joy and particular faith wording belong to their respective scenes.

The magistrates initially send officers with a release order. After Paul’s intervening protest, the magistrates come themselves and lead the men out. These are stages of the same release, with the changed personal involvement retained and no unreported reason supplied for the first order.

The jailer reports that the magistrates sent word for release, referring back to their order through the officers. His invitation to come out and go in peace is preserved as part of his speech, not treated as a second independently attested order or silently assigned wholly to the magistrates.

Paul protests public beating without a verdict despite Roman citizenship. In Jerusalem he questions scourging an uncondemned Roman citizen and the examination stops when his status becomes known. The first protest follows actual beating and speaks of the men plurally; the later scene concerns Paul before the planned scourging.

Philippi’s magistrates fear after hearing that the men are Romans. The Jerusalem tribune fears when he learns Paul is Roman and he had bound him. The shared reaction follows different restraints and information channels; the later verse does not independently identify Silas’s citizenship.

Paul had rejected secret dismissal and demanded that the officials come and lead the men out. They now come, appeal to them, lead them out and ask them to leave the city. The action answers that request; the edition’s appealed wording is not expanded into an explicit apology or legal verdict.

After prison the missionaries go to Lydia’s house, see and encourage the brothers, then depart. The earlier scene introduces Lydia’s faith, household baptism and invitation to stay with her. The named host and hospitality connect the visits without asserting an unreported building arrangement or identifying every brother as a household member.

Acts places the arrival at Thessalonica after the Philippian departure, naming Amphipolis and Apollonia along the way. The letter to the Thessalonians recalls coming to them after suffering at Philippi. It connects the mission sequence without supplying the intermediate towns or another travel date.

Paul customarily enters the synagogue and reasons from Scripture for three Sabbaths. Luke describes Jesus entering Nazareth’s synagogue on the Sabbath according to His custom and standing to read Isaiah. The shared Scripture-centered Sabbath setting does not identify the towns, speakers, readings or lengths of their visits.

Paul explains that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead and identifies the proclaimed Jesus as the Christ. Jesus’ words in Luke likewise state that the Christ should suffer and rise. Luke specifies the third day; that timing is not inserted into this Acts verse or treated as a quoted detail here.

In Thessalonica some are persuaded and join Paul and Silas, including devout Greeks and leading women. In Pisidian Antioch many Jews and devout converts follow Paul and Barnabas after the synagogue gathering. The responses connect, while the companions, audiences and convert descriptions are not equated.

Both scenes ascribe jealousy to local Jewish opponents of Paul’s preaching. Pisidian Antioch’s opponents contradict and abuse his words; Thessalonica’s gather marketplace men and attack Jason’s house. The different groups and actions remain particular episodes rather than an ethnic generalization.

At Philippi owners drag Paul and Silas before rulers and accuse them of disturbing the city. Here, when the missionaries are not found, Jason and other brothers are dragged before city officials and accused in connection with the missionaries. The arrested people, cities and actual charges differ.

The Thessalonian accusers say the people act against Caesar’s decrees by proclaiming another king, Jesus. In John, Jesus’ opponents tell Pilate that anyone making himself king speaks against Caesar. The shared political framing occurs in different accusations and does not turn either speech into a narrator-endorsed verdict.

The Thessalonian charge disturbs the crowd and city officials. At Philippi the forbidden-customs accusation is followed by the crowd joining an attack and magistrates ordering beatings. The responses are related but not identical: this verse does not say Jason or the brothers received the Philippian beating.

Brothers send Paul and Silas away by night toward Berea; Saul’s disciples earlier lower him through Damascus’s wall by night in a hamper. Both involve supporters enabling a threatened missionary’s night withdrawal, but the people, mechanism and destinations are distinct and no hamper is inserted into this journey.

The Bereans eagerly welcome the word and examine Scripture to test what they hear. In John Jesus says the hearers search the Scriptures that witness concerning Him yet are unwilling to come to Him for life. The passages connect Scripture and response to the message about Jesus without identifying the audiences or treating every examination as unbelief.

Both the Berean and Thessalonian accounts record belief or persuaded adherence involving Greeks and prominent women. The Berean wording follows their daily Scripture examination and also names men. The comparison retains distinct cities, groups and descriptions, rather than assigning the Bereans the exact numbers or response of Thessalonica.

Opponents travel from Thessalonica to Berea and disturb crowds against Paul’s preaching. Earlier Jews travel from Antioch and Iconium to Lystra, persuade the crowds and stone Paul. The cross-city pursuit is comparable, but this Berean verse does not report the earlier stoning or identify the opponents as the same people.

Brothers send Paul toward the sea while Silas and Timothy remain. Earlier, after a killing attempt, brothers bring Saul to Caesarea and send him to Tarsus. The supporters’ sending Paul away after opposition connects the accounts, while the routes and destinations differ; Acts17 does not specify a sea voyage or transfer the earlier companions into this scene.

Paul’s escorts carry a request for Silas and Timothy to join him quickly at Athens. The later narrative explicitly records those same two arriving from Macedonia while Paul is at Corinth. This follows their travel thread without asserting an unreported Athens visit, its absence, or the exact time they received and fulfilled the request.

Paul’s spirit is provoked by Athens’s idols. His later Athens argument rejects thinking of the divine nature as a humanly fashioned gold, silver or stone image. That argument addresses this observed setting; the later words are not inserted as a speech already delivered in this observation verse.

In Athens Paul reasons with Jews and worshipers in the synagogue and with passersby in the marketplace daily. In Corinth he reasons every Sabbath in the synagogue, seeking to persuade Jews and Greeks. The repeated activity connects his ministry, while the cities, audiences, venues and schedules remain distinct.

The narrator explains that the foreign-divinities accusation arose because Paul proclaimed Jesus and the resurrection. His earlier Thessalonian preaching explicitly identifies Jesus as the Christ who had to suffer and rise. The connection clarifies the proclaimed subject without endorsing the philosophers’ accusation or inventing a separate goddess called Resurrection.

The hearers bring Paul to the Areopagus asking to know his new teaching. The subsequent speech places him in the midst of the Areopagus and begins explaining the worship they do not know. This is the recorded response in that setting, not evidence that the invitation was a formal criminal trial.

Paul proclaims what the Athenians worship without knowing, beginning from an altar to an unknown god. Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that her group worships what it does not know and contrasts known worship and salvation from the Jews. The audiences and histories differ, and neither passage makes Athens and Samaria the same cult or endorses their objects of worship.

Paul says the Maker and Lord of heaven and earth does not dwell in handmade sanctuaries. Stephen says the Most High does not dwell in handmade things and quotes the heaven-throne, earth-footstool and divine-hand creation words. The shared claim has different audiences and formulations, rather than making Paul quote every line of Stephen’s speech.

Paul says God gives everyone life, breath and everything rather than needing human service. Isaiah describes the Maker of heaven and earth giving breath to earth’s people and spirit to those walking it. The life-giving claim connects; Isaiah’s verse does not independently supply Paul’s whole argument against treating God as needy.

Both passages describe divine ordering of nations and their boundaries. Deuteronomy names the Most High scattering the sons of Adam and setting bounds according to the angels of God; Acts says from one, with appointed times and dwelling boundaries. Acts’s unnamed one is not expanded into one blood, and Deuteronomy’s actual angels wording is not replaced with another edition.

Acts describes the nations’ purpose of seeking God and perhaps feeling toward and finding Him, who is not far away. Deuteronomy promises finding the Lord when the scattered people seek Him with their whole heart and soul in distress. The addressees, conditions and degree of assurance differ and are not combined into one quotation.

Paul speaks of living, moving and existing in God before citing the hearers’ poets about offspring. Job asks whether all living life and every human breath are in God’s hand. The dependence of life on God connects, while the hand and in-Him images differ; Job is not identified as the source of the quoted poets or of the offspring wording.

Paul rejects identifying the divine nature with gold, silver or stone shaped by human art and thought. Isaiah asks what likeness can represent the Lord and describes an artisan’s gold-gilded or wooden image. The critiques connect without adding Acts’s offspring argument or every named material to Isaiah’s different illustration.

Paul contrasts previously overlooked ignorance with God’s present command that all repent. At Lystra the missionaries urge turning to the Creator and say He formerly allowed nations to go their own ways while still giving witness through good gifts. These distinct speeches share past-versus-present framing without defining overlooked ignorance as approval, universal forgiveness or absence of every earlier witness.

Paul announces God’s fixed day of righteous judgment through an appointed Man, with resurrection as assurance. Peter’s preaching likewise identifies the One appointed by God as judge of living and dead. The appointment connects, while Acts17’s day, righteousness and assurance clauses are not quoted from Peter’s shorter formulation or used to supply a date.

Athens’s resurrection announcement meets mockery from some and a request for later hearing from others. Paul’s Corinthian argument challenges some saying there is no resurrection and explains the consequence for Christ’s resurrection and proclamation. The objection concerns the same subject, but the groups and responses are not identified or generalized to all Greeks.

Acts records Paul leaving Athens and coming to Corinth. His letter to Corinth recalls coming to its readers proclaiming God’s mystery and Jesus Christ crucified, in weakness and fear. The recollection connects his Corinth mission without supplying the Athens route or inserting those reported feelings into every step of the narrative arrival.

Acts introduces Aquila and his wife Priscilla, with Aquila’s Pontic origin and their departure from Italy under Claudius. The Corinthian letter sends greetings from Aquila and Prisca and the Church in their house. The paired names and ministry connect, with the Prisca/Priscilla forms retained; the letter does not repeat the expulsion or assign Aquila’s birthplace to his wife.

Paul works at the tentmaking trade shared with his Corinth hosts. In his later address to the Ephesian elders he says his hands served his own and his companions’ needs and urges work to support the weak. The common labor connects while the locations and descriptions differ; the later speech does not independently name tentmaking.

Both visits describe Paul reasoning in a synagogue on Sabbaths. Thessalonica specifies three Sabbaths and Scripture reasoning; Corinth says every Sabbath and persuasion directed to Jews and Greeks. The three-Sabbath count and exact audience are not transferred between the cities.

Silas and Timothy arrive from Macedonia while Paul is at Corinth, continuing the earlier request that they join him after he reached Athens. The names and travel thread connect; this notice does not establish whether they had also visited Athens or give an unreported itinerary between the two scenes.

At Corinth Paul responds to opposition by shaking his garments and saying he will go to the Gentiles. At Pisidian Antioch Paul and Barnabas announce a Gentile turn after rejection and later shake dust from their feet. The turns and gestures connect, but garments and feet are not made identical, nor are the opponents or places merged.

Paul tells the Corinthian opponents their blood is on their own heads and that he is clean. Later he declares himself clean from everyone’s blood because he did not withhold God’s whole purpose. The shared responsibility language has different audiences and scope; neither declaration is rewritten as Paul threatening physical violence.

Acts has Corinth’s synagogue ruler Crispus believe with his household and many Corinthians hear, believe and be baptized. Paul’s letter to Corinth names Crispus among the few he personally baptized. The named Corinthian connection is precise, but the letter does not repeat Crispus’s office or say Paul personally baptized every Corinthian or every member of Crispus’s household.

The Lord tells Paul in a Corinth night vision to keep speaking without fear. On the later night in Jerusalem the Lord stands beside him, gives courage and speaks of witness in Rome. The encounters share encouragement for witness, but Acts23 is not silently labeled the same vision or given Corinth’s particular promise.

The Corinth vision assures Paul of the Lord’s presence, protection from harm there and many people in that city. Isaiah’s servant-address assurance likewise announces God’s presence and describes His having strengthened, helped and secured the recipient. The addressees and specific protections differ; no general promise that Paul or every believer will never suffer injury is inferred.

Acts specifies a year and six months of Paul teaching in Corinth, and later two years of the Ephesian instruction through which Asia hears the word. These are distinct location-specific time notices, not interchangeable totals or evidence that every period of Paul’s wider ministry lasted the same time.

Paul is brought before Gallio’s tribunal in Achaia by local Jewish accusers. The later Caesarean scene has the seated governor order Paul brought before him and Jerusalem accusers make charges. The Roman hearing settings connect without identifying the governors, accusers, charges or outcomes.

The Corinthian accusers say Paul persuades unlawful worship. In Jerusalem opponents accuse him of teaching against the people, law and temple, adding an alleged Greek entry. These are different reported accusations, not narrator verdicts; the temple allegation and its stated supposition are not inserted into Gallio’s case.

Gallio distinguishes an ordinary wrong or wicked crime, which he would hear, from the dispute actually presented. Festus later says he expected evil charges but instead found disputes about the accusers’ religion and Jesus’ being alive. The assessments are by different officials; Gallio’s conditional statement is not converted into Festus’s actual report or a universal legal rule.

Gallio calls the case questions of words, names and the accusers’ own law and refuses to judge them. The tribune’s later letter likewise describes questions of their law, but explicitly finds no charge deserving death or imprisonment. The religious-dispute characterization connects while the separate officials’ conclusions retain their actual scope.

Gallio’s driving the accusers from the tribunal follows his stated refusal to judge their questions of words, names and law. The statement and narrated action belong to the same hearing; the action is not expanded into an acquittal on every possible charge or a general religious policy.

The departure notice includes a haircut at Cenchreae because of a vow. The later Jerusalem instructions concern four men under a vow, purification, expenses and head shaving. The related vow-and-hair practices are compared without identifying the vows, resolving the source pronoun beyond its wording, or declaring an unstated Nazirite duration or procedure.
